claims.text: The paper addresses scale imbalance in multi-target semi-supervised medical image segmentation: large targets may receive priority, causing smaller targets and background to be misclassified as larger structures.

CGS uses a teacher–student framework with weak-to-strong consistency, a general segmentation branch, and class-specific specialist heads that distinguish background, their target class, and all remaining target classes.
The teacher is updated by exponential moving average of the student; supervised and unsupervised segmentation losses combine cross-entropy and Dice losses.
Bidirectional cross-branch consistency exchanges pseudo-labels between the generalist and specialists, while a consensus-based loss jointly optimizes regions where the branches agree.
IHED filters specialist pseudo-labels using inter-head agreement: either every head predicts background, or one head predicts its target and all other heads predict their remaining classes.

ACDC contains scans from 100 patients with three segmentation targets and uses a 7:1:2 training/validation/test split. SegTHOR has four targets and 28/4/8 training/validation/test volumes. Synapse contains 30 CT scans annotated with eight abdominal organs and uses 18 training and 12 test cases. Input slices are resized to 224 × 224.
Experiments use three different seeds on each of the three datasets and report means and standard deviations.
On ACDC, CGS achieves DSC of 88.83±0.14% with 3 labeled scans (5%) and 89.83±0.11% with 7 labeled scans (10%), compared with FixMatch's 87.27% and 88.89%, respectively.
On SegTHOR, CGS achieves DSC of 81.74±1.29% with 3 labeled scans (10%) and 83.69±1.45% with 6 labeled scans (20%), compared with FixMatch's 79.38% and 81.94%, respectively.

On Synapse with 3 labeled volumes, CGS achieves average DSC of 60.20±0.37% and average HD95 of 61.40±1.04, compared with FixMatch's 58.33% and 80.79. CGS does not improve every organ: its left-kidney and spleen DSC values are 65.39% and 61.89%, versus FixMatch's 71.71% and 69.15%.
At ACDC's 5% labeled setting, CGS has worse 95HD than BCP: 2.42±0.08 versus 1.90.
Training memory increases with the number of classes: at batch size 24 with teacher and student networks, reported GPU memory rises from 7.13 GB for 3 classes to 10.62 GB for 8 classes.
The authors state that IHED and cross-branch consistency depend on the specialized segmentation heads, preventing independent ablations of these modules without that foundation.
More comprehensive simultaneous handling of occurrence and scale imbalance remains future work; adding resampling to CGS raises Synapse average DSC from 60.20% to 64.93%.

The authors present CGS, its cross-branch consistency losses, and IHED as contributions for more balanced training and improved pseudo-labels. Specialists are discarded at inference, so the collaboration occurs during training and inference uses the general branch without additional specialist memory or time costs.
